title: The moon can't be stolen
hook: the hermit Ryokan gives a thief his clothes and wishes he could give him the moon (Zen story, Japan)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hakuin met blame and apology with the same three words. Your line was is that so. When did you say it inside? Day forty-six.

One room. A straw roof. A bowl, a cushion, a few poems written on scraps of paper. That was the hut of Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived alone at the foot of a mountain in Japan. Tradition remembers him playing with the village children and begging for his rice, and his poems are still read today. One evening, while Ryokan is out walking, a thief slips into the hut, looking for something to steal. There is nothing. Then Ryokan comes home, and finds him. Today's story is the moon can't be stolen.
screen: `ONE ROOM, A STRAW ROOF.` → `RYOKAN, MONK AND POET.` → `A THIEF IN THE EMPTY HUT.`

segments.voice: The thief is caught. And Ryokan isn't angry. He's sorry. You've come such a long way to visit me, he says, and you shouldn't go home empty-handed. Please, take my clothes. And he takes off the robe he's wearing and hands it over. The thief, bewildered, grabs the clothes and runs off into the dark. Ryokan sits down, naked, in his doorway, and looks up at the night. The moon is rising, huge and bright. And he says to himself: poor fellow. I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon. The story is usually tied to a short poem that Japanese tradition credits to Ryokan: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. Scholars can't say for sure the robbery happened just this way, but the poem and the story have traveled together for a long time. Now look at what Ryokan knows. The thief came for things. Ryokan barely had any, and gave away the last of them without a fight. What he actually treasured, the thief couldn't carry off, because it wasn't his to keep in the first place. The moon doesn't belong to anyone. It shines on the hut and the thief's road the same. Ryokan's wish is the whole teaching: he wants the thief to have what he himself has. Not the robe. The seeing. The quiet. A night bright enough to be rich in. We guard our things carefully, and they can be lost. The moon stays.
screen: `TAKE MY CLOTHES.` · `I WISH I COULD GIVE HIM THE MOON.` · `THE THIEF LEFT IT BEHIND.` · `WHAT CAN'T BE CARRIED OFF.` · then, large: `THE MOON STAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give one thing freely today. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of something you have that no one could steal: a view you love, a memory, a skill, the fact that you're breathing. Rest in it for a moment. Then think of one small thing you could give away today, with nothing asked back. A coat you don't wear. Your time. A kind word to someone who didn't earn it. Decide when you'll give it. Then let it go already, in your mind, the way Ryokan let go of his robe. The bell holds the time.
The moon can't be stolen. Ryokan gives a thief his clothes, and wishes he could give him the moon. Today's word.
screen: `THE MOON CAN'T BE STOLEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the moon stays. Today, give one thing freely, and don't count it as lost. Ryokan didn't. Day forty-six.

howItsDone: Ryokan is remembered in Japan as a poet-monk of simple living, and Zen teachers tell the story of the thief and the moon when talking about generosity and letting go of possessions.

what it means: what we most treasure can't be taken, and Ryokan wants even the thief to have it.

notes: Ryokan (Ryōkan Taigu, 1758–1831), Sōtō Zen monk and poet, hut on Mount Kugami: described generally as 'around the year 1800' and 'at the foot of a mountain'. Confirm.
The poem usually given as 盗人に取り残されし窓の月 is paraphrased ('the thief left it behind, the moon in my window'), not quoted. Confirm the attribution to Ryokan and the paraphrase.
The Zen Flesh, Zen Bones telling is not public domain; paraphrased.
